title: Reading & Building Numbers from Place Value
technique: Decompose H/T/U; form the largest or smallest number from a given set of digits; read a value description and name the number.

blocks.title: Challenge First
blocks.note: Original hook questions. Students attempt cold. Hint ladder appears after 2 min.

questions.question: Mia has three digit cards: [card:8], [card:3], and [card:5]. She uses each card exactly once to make a 3-digit number. What is the LARGEST number she can make?
questions.explanation: Put the largest digit (8) in hundreds, next (5) in tens, smallest (3) in ones → 853.

onWrong.feedback: The hundreds column holds the most value — putting a small digit there wastes it. Try again with the biggest card in hundreds.

hints: Which position is worth the most? Put the biggest digit there.
Think of the hundreds column as the VIP seat — the digit there is worth 100 times more. Which card deserves it?

questions.question: Using the same three cards [card:8], [card:3], and [card:5], make the SMALLEST 3-digit number.
questions.explanation: Put the smallest digit (3) in hundreds, next (5) in tens, largest (8) in ones → 358.

onWrong.feedback: You want the number to be as small as possible. Start by giving the hundreds position the smallest card you have.

hints: Now you want the hundreds digit to be as small as possible.
You have picked the hundreds digit. Now look at what is left — which one should go to tens to keep the number small?

blocks.title: Place Value in Action
blocks.note: Spine: 3 techniques — decompose into H/T/Ones, build largest/smallest from given digits, read a value description and name the number. CPA per section: Concrete (figure) → Pictorial (applet) → Abstract (apply). Three applets: place-value-chart on 777, digit-rearranger on digits 4,0,7, number-builder on 603/480/205. Visual-first, no passive cards.

steps.title: Three digits. Smallest number?
steps.text: Using the digits 4, 0, and 8 once each, what is the smallest 3-digit number you can make?

onCorrect.feedback: Sharp — you spotted the rule that catches everyone off guard.

onWrong.feedback: Most folks try 048 — but '048' is just 48, a 2-digit number. We will fix this in five minutes.

steps.title: Same digit. Three places. Three values.
steps.text: The same 7 sits in three columns — and means three completely different things.
steps.keyInsight: Each step left: ×10. Each step right: ÷10.

endQuestion.prompt: The hundreds 7 is worth {blank} times the ones 7.

steps.title: Tap each column
steps.instruction: Tap each of the three columns to reveal what its 7 is worth.

discoveryQuestion.prompt: Adjacent columns always differ by a factor of {blank}.

steps.discoveryMessage: 700 ÷ 70 = 10.   70 ÷ 7 = 10.   Every step left is exactly 10× more valuable.

steps.title: Read every digit's value in 749
steps.text: Same rule, fresh number. Read each digit's value, one column at a time.

onAllCorrect.summary: You can read any digit's value.
onAllCorrect.feedback: Now — what if you're handed loose digits and asked to build a number?

steps.title: Sort the digits. Big lives left.
steps.text:
You just learned what each column is worth. Now use that — to build numbers.

The Hundreds column multiplies by 100, the Ones column by 1. So the biggest digit always belongs in Hundreds — that's the seat with the most leverage.
steps.keyInsight: Largest: sort high to low. Smallest: sort low to high; zero takes Tens or Ones, never Hundreds.

endQuestion.prompt: Using digits 3, 8, 1 once each, the largest 3-digit number is {blank}.

steps.title: Drag and drop
steps.instruction: Drag the digits 4, 0, 7 into Hundreds, Tens, Ones to make the smallest 3-digit number. Then do it again for the largest.
steps.discoveryMessage: Tempting to put 0 first — but '047' is just 47. The next-smallest digit (4) takes the hundreds seat. Zero slides to tens.

steps.title: Three quick checks
steps.text: Three quick checks — make sure largest and smallest are locked in, including the leading-zero trap.

steps.hint: Biggest digit in hundreds, then tens, then ones.
Zero can't lead — 3 takes hundreds, 0 slides to tens.

onAllCorrect.feedback: Last move — read a description and name the number.

steps.title: When zero shows up
steps.text:
You can decompose. You can build. Now — read a description and name the number.

408 = 400 + 0 + 8. The zero says "nothing in tens" — but it keeps 4 and 8 exactly where they belong. Lose the zero and you get 48. Same digits, completely different number.
steps.keyInsight: Zero is not missing — it is working. It holds a place.

steps.title: Build each number
steps.instruction: Try it yourself — three targets, each with a zero in a different spot. Press + / − to build each one. Watch the expanded form update as you go.

discoveryQuestion.prompt: In 603, the value of the tens digit is {blank}.

steps.discoveryMessage:
603 = 600 + 0 + 3.   480 = 400 + 80 + 0.   205 = 200 + 0 + 5.
Zero keeps every other digit exactly in place.

steps.title: Three quick checks
steps.text: Three quick checks — make sure expanded form (with zeros) and value-description naming are locked in.

steps.hint: 4 hundreds = 400. 8 tens = 80. 0 ones = 0. Add them in that order.
Hundreds = 300, tens = 0, ones = 6 — put them together.

steps.prompt: A number has 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 9 ones. The number is {blank}.

rules.name: Build largest/smallest
rules.statement: sort Hundreds → Tens → Ones; zero never leads

rules.name: Read & name
rules.statement: X Hundreds, Y Tens, Z Ones → X×100 + Y×10 + Z

curiosity.reveal: That 12 is called the digit sum. It ignores position — but it reveals hidden properties that competition questions love to exploit. That's the first thing Lesson 1.2 unpacks. →

place-value-ratio.title: Quick refresher — the 10× rule
place-value-ratio.text: Each step left is 10× more valuable. 700 ÷ 70 = 10. 70 ÷ 7 = 10. So hundreds is 10× tens, and tens is 10× ones.

miniCheck.prompt: The hundreds digit is worth ___ times the ones digit.

place-value-decompose.title: Walk through one digit at a time
place-value-decompose.text: To find a digit's value: read its place. Hundreds digit × 100. Tens digit × 10. Ones digit × 1.

miniCheck.prompt: In 853, the value of digit 5 is ___.

largest-smallest-formation.title: Sort it. Then watch for zero.
largest-smallest-formation.text: To build the largest number, sort the digits high to low across Hundreds, Tens, Ones. To build the smallest, sort low to high — but zero can't lead, because '047' is just 47.

miniCheck.feedback: To build the smallest, sort low to high — but 0 can't lead. So 4 takes hundreds, 0 takes tens, 7 takes ones → 407.

expanded-form-zero-placeholder.title: Zero holds a place — it never disappears
expanded-form-zero-placeholder.text: When a column has 0, the 0 stays in its place. 408 has 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 8 ones → 400 + 0 + 8. Drop the 0 and you get 48 — a completely different number.

problem.question: Jackie wants to place the digit 3 somewhere in the number 2014. Where should she place the digit 3 to make the resulting five-digit number as small as possible?

narrationSegments.content: Jackie inserts digit 3 into 2014. The digit can go in any gap.

question.question: How many different positions can digit 3 be inserted? {blank}
hints: Count: before 2, between 2–0, between 0–1, between 1–4, after 4.
question.explanation: 4 digits → 5 gaps: one before the first digit, one between each adjacent pair, one after the last.

scaffoldedSteps.title: Map each slot to its number

question.question: Slot C (between 0 and 1) gives the number {blank}.
hints: Insert 3 between 0 and 1: 2 · 0 · _ · 1 · 4

question.question: Slot D (between 1 and 4) gives the number {blank}.
hints: Insert 3 between 1 and 4: 2 · 0 · 1 · _ · 4

narrationSegments.content: Goal: smallest. Compare digit by digit from the left.
items: B, C, D, E · first digit = 2

question.question: After eliminating A, how many candidates remain?
hints: Started with 5 slots; crossed out 1.
question.explanation: Remove A → B, C, D, E remain. 4 candidates.

narrationSegments.content: Compare B, C, D, E by second digit:
Compare C, D, E by third digit:

question.question: Second digit of 23014 is {blank}.
hints: Read 23014 left to right: digit 1=2, digit 2=?

question.question: Two options remain. Which are they?
hints: A, B, C were eliminated. What is left from the five?
question.explanation: Eliminated A (first digit), B (second digit), C (third digit). Remaining: D (20134) and E (20143).

scaffoldedSteps.title: Final comparison + insight

narrationSegments.content: D vs E — same first three digits. Compare fourth:
items: 3 < 4 → D wins. Answer: place 3 between 1 and 4 → 20134

narrationSegments.content: Insight: to minimise, push the inserted digit rightward past all original digits smaller than it.

question.question: Which is smaller: 20134 or 20143?
hints: First three digits are identical. Compare the fourth.
question.explanation: Fourth digit: 20134 has 3, 20143 has 4. Since 3 < 4, 20134 is smaller.

question.question: What if Jackie wanted the LARGEST number instead?
hints: To maximise, the leftmost position should hold the biggest digit. Is 3 > 2?
question.explanation: 3 > 2, so placing 3 in ten-thousands gives 32014 — larger than any option where 2 leads.

scaffoldedSteps.insight: To minimise an inserted digit's effect, push it as far right as possible past smaller digits. To maximise, push it as far left as possible past smaller digits.

problem.question: Which four digits need to be removed from the number 4921508 to get the smallest possible three-digit number?

narrationSegments.content: 7 digits. Remove exactly 4, keep 3. Kept digits stay in original left-to-right order — no rearranging.

question.question: Keeping positions 4, 6, 7 from 4921508 gives digits 1, 0, 8. What 3-digit number is that? {blank}
hints: Digits 1, 0, 8 in left-to-right order = one hundred and eight.

narrationSegments.content: Minimise → smallest hundreds digit. Rule: it must have at least 2 digits to its right.
items: Positions 1–5: each has 2+ digits to the right
Position 6 (digit 0): only 1 digit to the right

narrationSegments.content: Valid positions for hundreds: 1–5, with digits 4, 9, 2, 1, 5.

question.question: How many digits are to the right of position 5 in 4921508? {blank}
hints: Position 5 is the fifth digit. Count positions 6 and 7.
question.explanation: Positions 6 (digit 0) and 7 (digit 8) are to the right → 2 digits.

question.question: Smallest digit among 4, 9, 2, 1, 5 is {blank}.
hints: Compare all five: 1, 2, 4, 5, 9.
question.explanation: Smallest is 1. It sits at position 4.

narrationSegments.content: Hundreds = 1 (position 4). Scan right for tens — needs 1 digit further to its right.
Tens = 0 (position 6). Only digit to the right is 8 (position 7) → ones = 8.

question.question: Which tens digit gives the smaller final number?
hints: Compare 158 and 108.

question.question: The smallest 3-digit subsequence from 4921508 is {blank}.
hints: Hundreds=1, Tens=0, Ones=8.

narrationSegments.content: Kept: positions 4, 6, 7 → digits 1, 0, 8. Removed: positions 1, 2, 3, 5 → digits 4, 9, 2, 5.

question.question: Which answer option lists the four removed digits?
hints: Kept digits are 1, 0, 8. Everything else in 4 9 2 1 5 0 8 was removed.

blocks.title: Practice Lab
blocks.note: Problems 1–3: direct application, 3pt. Problems 4–6: two-step or slight twist, 4pt. Problems 7–8: competition-authentic, no scaffolding, 4pt. Hints available on all.

problems.question: Sam has three digit cards: 4, 7, and 9. She uses each card exactly once. What is the LARGEST 3-digit number she can make?
problems.explanation: To make the largest number, put the biggest digit (9) in hundreds, then 7 in tens, then 4 in ones → 974.
hints: Hundreds is worth the most. Which digit is biggest — give it the hundreds position.
After placing the largest digit in hundreds, assign the next largest to tens.
After 9 in hundreds and 7 in tens, only one card is left — which slot does it fill?

problems.question: About the number 325, five boys said: Andy: "This is a 3-digit number." Barry: "All the digits are different." Charlie: "The sum of the digits is 10." Danny: "The ones digit is 5." Eddie: "All the digits are odd." Which of the boys was wrong?
problems.explanation: 325: Andy (3-digit, correct). Barry (digits 3, 2, 5 are all different, correct). Charlie (3+2+5=10, correct). Danny (ones digit 5, correct). Eddie — digit 2 is even, so not all digits are odd.
hints: Check each claim one at a time.
Is every digit of 325 an odd number? What are the three digits?
The digits are 3, 2, and 5. Is 2 odd or even?

problems.question: What is the largest digit that can replace the blank in 6_3 so that 6_3 < 670?
problems.explanation: If tens = 6: 663 < 670 correct. If tens = 7: 673 > 670 incorrect. Largest valid tens digit = 6.
hints: Compare the tens digit: what value keeps 6_3 less than 670?
You tried tens = 6 and tens = 7. Which of those results is still less than 670?

problems.question: We add 17 to the smallest two-digit number and then divide the sum by the largest one-digit number. What is the result?
hints: What is the smallest two-digit number? What is the largest one-digit number?
Smallest 2-digit = 10. Largest 1-digit = 9. Now compute (10 + 17) ÷ 9.
What is 27 divided by 9?

problems.question: In the number 528, by how much does the value of digit 5 exceed the value of digit 2?
problems.explanation: 5 is in hundreds → value = 500. 2 is in tens → value = 20. 500 − 20 = 480.
hints: What is the value of digit 5 in 528? What is the value of digit 2 in 528?
Value of 5 (hundreds) = 500. Value of 2 (tens) = 20. Find the difference.
You have both values. Now subtract the smaller from the larger.

problems.question: David wrote a one-digit number, and next to it to the right he wrote another digit to form a two-digit number. Then he added 19 to this number and the sum was 72. What was the first digit he wrote?
problems.explanation: Two-digit number + 19 = 72 → number = 53. First digit = tens digit = 5.
hints: Work backwards: two-digit number = 72 − 19. What is that number?
The first digit David wrote becomes the tens digit of the two-digit number.
What is the tens digit of the two-digit number you just found?

problems.question: Leo inserts the digit 5 somewhere into the number 37 to make a 3-digit number. What is the SMALLEST 3-digit number he can make?
problems.explanation: Three positions: 537 (5 in front), 357 (5 between 3 and 7), 375 (5 at end). Smallest = 357.
hints: List all three positions for 5: before 3, between 3 and 7, after 7.
Compare: 537, 357, 375. Which is smallest?
Compare your three options starting from the left — which one has the smallest hundreds digit?

problems.question: Tom has four digit cards: 7, 0, 3, 5. What is the LARGEST possible 4-digit number he can make (0 cannot go in the thousands place)?
problems.explanation: 0 cannot lead a 4-digit number. Digits largest to smallest: 7, 5, 3, 0 → 7530.
hints: Try placing 7 in thousands. Then arrange 5, 3, 0 from largest to smallest in remaining places.
Watch out: can 0 go in thousands place?
With 7 in thousands, arrange the remaining three digits from largest to smallest in the next positions.

blocks.title: Mastery Check
blocks.note: 4 original questions. No hints. Pass 3/4 to unlock Lesson 1.2. On fail: returned to Practice Lab.

questions.question: What is the LARGEST 3-digit number that can be made from digits 6, 0, and 4 (each used once)?
questions.explanation: Largest digit (6) → hundreds, next (4) → tens, 0 → ones → 640. Note: 0 cannot go in hundreds.

questions.question: What is the smallest 3-digit number that can be made using digits 3, 8, and 1 (each used once)?
questions.explanation: Smallest non-zero digit (1) → hundreds, next smallest (3) → tens, largest (8) → ones → 138.

questions.question: Maya has three digit cards: 3, 6, 1. Which arrangement gives the SMALLEST 3-digit number?
questions.explanation: Smallest non-zero digit (1) → hundreds, next (3) → tens, largest (6) → ones → 136. Option A.

questions.question: Digit card 4 is placed to the right of digit card 7 to make the number 74. What is 74 minus (7 times 7)?

blocks.title: Challenge Extension
blocks.note: One hard problem beyond the lesson level. Always accessible — never gated by the mastery check result.

problems.question: An electronic watch indicates the time 02:07. After how much time will the same digits show up again for the first time, not necessarily in the same order?
problems.explanation: At 02:07 the four displayed digits are 0, 2, 0, 7. Valid times from digits 0, 0, 2, 7: 00:27 (before), 07:02, 07:20, 20:07. First valid time after 02:07 is 07:02. Elapsed: 4 hours 55 minutes.
hints: List the four digits shown at 02:07. You need 0, 0, 2, and 7.
What valid times (HH:MM, from 00:00 to 23:59) can be formed using exactly these four digits?
You have your list of valid times. Now scan through them in order — which is the first one that appears after 02:07 on the clock?
